title: YouTube Canada’s Slate of Creator Shows to Include a Series of Kareem Rahma’s ‘SubwayTakes’ in Toronto
description:
Sep 17, 2026 3:30pm PT	
	

	
		YouTube Canada’s Slate of Creator Shows to Include a Series of Kareem Rahma’s ‘SubwayTakes’ in Toront
body:
Sep 17, 2026 3:30pm PT	
	

	
		YouTube Canada’s Slate of Creator Shows to Include a Series of Kareem Rahma’s ‘SubwayTakes’ in Toronto
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Brian Karlsson
	

		
	
				
	At its annual YouTube Features marketing showcase in Toronto, YouTube Canada unveiled a slate of new Canadian creator shows — including a run of Kareem Rahma‘s popular interview show “SubwayTakes” in the Great White North.

	Rahma, who served as the host of Thursday’s YouTube Features event, is behind hit show “SubwayTakes,” in which he gets hot takes from people riding on the New York City subway. The show has more than 1.1 million subscribers on YouTube and 800 million views to date.
	

	Set to premiere in 2027, “SubwayTakes Toronto” will see Rahma take the unfiltered, long-form interview series to the Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) subway system. Each episode will feature “iconic Canadian guests” and bring viewers “viewer directly in the middle of the authentic, unscripted mayhem found inside Canada’s most recognizable subway car,” according to YouTube Canada.


	Alongside “SubwayTakes Toronto,” the YouTube Canada slate of upcoming creator programming includes a new video podcast from Olympic gold medal figure skater Tessa Virtue; a trends-focused food show from chef and restaurateur Susur Lee and his son Jet Bent-Lee; and a reality series from beloved Canadian comedian Jeenie Weenie.



	

	



	These follow the slate of creator-led shows announced at 2026 YouTube Brandcast earlier this year, including Rahma’s “Keep the Meter Running” and programs from Alex Cooper and Trevor Noah.

	“YouTube creators are making the must-see programming that is shaping culture and redefining entertainment,” said Nicole Bell, head of YouTube Canada. “With this new slate, we’re proud to invest in homegrown creative entrepreneurs, giving Canada’s most compelling storytellers the opportunity to bring their biggest ideas to life and connect directly with the audiences who love them.”
	

	Here’s a rundown of the new creator shows announced Thursday coming exclusively to YouTube:


Iron Chef Dad: “Iron Chef Dad vs. The Internet”: Susur Lee’s son, Jet Bent-Lee, introduces his chef dad to the viral recipes, food trends, hacks, restaurant items and snacks dominating online conversation. Each episode takes the father and son duo into a new corner of internet food culture; from fast-food items and grocery-store snacks to food challenges and international dishes as Susur tastes, reacts and offers his candid perspective on what works and what doesn’t. Along the way, he may reimagine a dish, create his own version or explain how he would approach it differently. At its core, the series explores what happens when a celebrated chef and his son take on the ever-evolving world of internet food.
Jeenie Weenie: “Roots”: Known to their 13 million subscribers for their sketch comedy, Jeenie and Johnny step back from viral hits to reconnect with their Korean heritage as new parents. Together, they navigate what it means to pass on their culture, food, language and traditions to their daughter, Nari. Each episode follows a different part of that journey, from trips and recipes to family rituals and everyday discoveries as they build the world, they want her to grow up in. At its heart, the series is an intimate look at two creators exploring identity, family and heritage in real time as they become the parents, they want to be.
Julie Nolke: “Becky and Miranda”: In a dark comedy about the bonds of friendship, Becky and Miranda are two everyday millennial women navigating dating burnout, career pressure, and modern womanhood — who also happen to share an outrageous penchant for serial killing. As the duo bond over the absurd logistics of their lethal hobby and evade detection, the series uses its heightened premise to deliver a hilarious, deeply relatable exploration of female friendship and unconditional loyalty. Created by Julie Nolke (Run the Burbs) and starring Nolke alongside Nicole Power (Kim’s Convenience).
Matty Matheson & Super Athletic Film Co.: “Matty’s Farm”: From the minds of Matty Matheson, Ricky Staffieri and Super Athletic Film Co., comes a new heartfelt series set in rural Ontario. This time, chef, restaurateur and hometown hero Matheson is going all in. He’s building, growing, expanding — and turning a farm dream into a reality.
Alexandra Gater: “Dream Apartment Makeover” Season 3: Gater and her team once again gift a deserving subscriber a complete, multi-room apartment transformation. Building on the emotional connection audiences formed with the series’ first two seasons, each makeover goes beyond a new look to explore how an intentionally designed home can support someone through a major life change. The series began with Kate, who was nominated by friends following her MS diagnosis, and whose story resonated deeply with viewers as they followed her transformation room by room.
Sarah Nurse: “Sarah’s Side Quests”: In this series, Olympian and pro hockey star Sarah spends her offseason learning new skills from some of Canada’s top athletes, experts and creators, building on her love of trying different sports and taking on new challenges. Each episode pairs her with a guest who teaches her the ins and outs of their craft, while natural conversations reveal their personal journeys, mindsets and experiences.
Tessa Virtue: “Virtuoso”: The new podcast series about the pursuit of mastery is hosted by Virtue, a retired ice dancer who is a five-time Olympic medalist and three-time World Champion. She uses her sports background to explore unique interpretations of excellence. She talks to her guests candidly and with relatable personal experience, creating an atmosphere grounded in trust and authenticity. Drawing on the teamwork and discipline that defined her record-breaking career, she invites guests into conversations that feel less like interviews and more like meaningful exchanges between peers. Each episode, Tessa sits down with athletes, artists, entrepreneurs, scientists, leaders, and creators to explore the experiences, decisions, and relationships that have shaped them. Watch the trailer at this link.
Sunday Kalogeras, Demitra Kalogeras, Eliana Kalogeras (Kalogeras Sisters): “Hardly Workin”: Three designer-clad sisters clock in for full shifts at jobs they are spectacularly unqualified for. Inspired by The Simple Life and reimagined for Gen Z, Hardly Workin’ throws the glamorous trio into demanding, unpredictable situations, letting their signature chaos and charm unfold in real time. The Kalogeras sisters take their personality-driven comedy to the next level: each episode drops them into an unfamiliar industry with zero prep, no shortcuts, and luxury clutches strictly optional.

title: Netflix Orders Dark Comedy ‘All the Rage’ From ‘Dead to Me’ Duo Liz Feldman, Kelly Hutchinson
description: Liz Feldman has extended her overall deal with Netflix, with the streamer greenlighting the dark comedy “All the Rage” with Feldman onboard as co-cr
body:
Liz Feldman has extended her overall deal with Netflix, with the streamer greenlighting the dark comedy “All the Rage” with Feldman onboard as co-creator. 

	“All the Rage” hails from Feldman and Kelly Hutchinson, who previously worked with Feldman on the Netflix shows “Dead to Me” and “No Good Deed.” Both are also executive producers. Will Ferrell and Jessica Elbaum executive produce via Gloria Sanchez Productions, with Christie Smith of Rise Management also executive producing. All three were executive producers on “Dead to Me” and “No Good Deed.” 
	

	The logline for “All the Rage” states that it centers on Emma and Eli, “old friends who reconnect after a long estrangement and find new purpose in taking down the man who tore them apart.” 


	“We’re thrilled to tell this completely made up story about revenge inspired by our very real friendship of 30 years,” Feldman and Hutchinson said in a joint statement. “Thank you to Netflix for being the best partners in the biz and, more importantly, for paying us to finally work through 30 years of neurosis and resentment.” 

	“Dead to Me” aired for three seasons on Netflix and starred Christina Applegate and Linda Cardellini as two women who are part of the same grief support group. The show proved to be a critical hit for the streamer, earning six Emmy nominations over its run. That includes nominations for both Cardellini and Applegate as well as one for outstanding comedy series. 

	“No Good Deed” followed in 2024. That series was an ensemble whose cast included Lisa Kudrow, Ray Romano, Cardellini, Luke Wilson, O-T Fagbenle, Abbi Jacobson, Denis Leary, Poppy Liu, and Teyonah Parris. 
	

	“We’re excited to continue our partnership with Liz and bring more of her distinct, brilliant vision to audiences worldwide,” said Tracey Pakosta, Netflix vice president of comedy series. “Her decades-long friendship with Kelly fuels their unique and sharp creative chemistry, which they showcased during their collaboration on ‘Dead to Me.’ We’re thrilled to have them join forces again for All the Rage, which is sure to blend dark comedy and emotional depth like only Liz and Kelly can.” 

	Feldman is repped by CAA, Rise Management, and Yorn Levine Barnes. Hutchinson is repped by UTA, SEL Media Group, and Goodman Genow. Ferrell and Elbaum are repped by UTA, with Ferrell also repped by Mosaic and Jackoway Austen Tyerman.

title: ‘Far Cry’ FX Series Casts Brendan Gleeson, Jennifer Jason Leigh, Hamish Linklater, Sam Spruell, Jamie Demetriou
description:
The “Far Cry” TV series at FX is continuing to build out an all-star cast. 

	Variety has learned that Brendan Gleeson (“The Banshees of Inisherin,”
body:
The “Far Cry” TV series at FX is continuing to build out an all-star cast. 

	Variety has learned that Brendan Gleeson (“The Banshees of Inisherin,” “In Bruges”), Jennifer Jason Leigh (“The Hateful Eight,” FX’s “Fargo”), Hamish Linklater (“Widow’s Bay,” “Midnight Mass”), Sam Spruell (“A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms,” FX’s “Alien: Earth”), and Jamie Demetriou (“Stath Lets Flats,” “The Afterparty”) are all set to appear in the first season of the series, which is based on the video game franchise of the same name.
	

	The five new additions join previously announced lead and co-creator Rob Mac and fellow cast members Lizzy Caplan and Steve Buscemi.


	The series was first reported to be set up at FX in November 2025 from creators Noah Hawley and Mac. Exact plot and character details remain under wraps, but the series will follow an anthology format like the “Far Cry” games and feature a different cast and setting each season.

	“Far Cry” will air on FX, Hulu, and Disney+ internationally. Mac will executive produce under his More Better Productions banner, while Hawley will executive produce under his overall deal with FX and Disney Entertainment Television via 26 Keys. Simon Emanuel will also executive produce along with Emilia Serrano for 26 Keys, Nick Frenkel for 3 Arts, Monica Macer, Peter Calloway, John Campisi, and Gerard Guillemot, Margaret Boykin and Austin Dill for Ubisoft Film & Television. The series will be produced by FX Productions.

	Gleeson is repped by CAA and Principal Entertainment. Leigh is repped by by CAA and Untitled Entertainment. Linklater is repped by Untitled Entertainment, Gersh and Johnson Shapiro Slewett & Kole. Spruell is repped by Lou Coulson Associates and Luber Roklin Entertainment. Demetriou is repped by United Agents, CAA, and Multitude Media.

title: ‘Evil Genius’ Review: Courteney Cox Fashions the Pizza Bomber Case Into a Broad, Shrilly Played Farce
description: If you were glued to “Evil Genius,” Netflix’s 2018 documentary series about the bizarre “pizza bomber” killing of 2003, but wished its true-crime st
body:
If you were glued to “Evil Genius,” Netflix’s 2018 documentary series about the bizarre “pizza bomber” killing of 2003, but wished its true-crime study rang just a little less true, then Courteney Cox’s new film of the same title has you covered. Dramatizing that sad, sordid story of weaponized criminal incompetence into a heightened comedy of errors, the film has little to reveal that we don’t already know, so settles for raking over the stranger-than-fiction facts of the case with lurid, mocking glee. Viewers’ mileage will largely depend on their patience for Patricia Arquette’s unmodulated, to-the-rafters performance as the scheme’s criminal not-so-mastermind Marjorie Diehl-Armstrong, which is scarcely tempered by David Harbour’s more quietly shambling work as her co-conspirator and sometime lover Bill Rothstein.
	

	Assembled with little formal style or finesse by Cox — in her first feature-length directorial effort since 2014’s Seann William Scott comedy “Just Before I Go” — this very broad affair likely has a built-in audience of rubberneckers, given the level of public fascination that this case has maintained in the U.S. for over 20 years. But it’s doubtful that many would venture out to a theater to see a rehash of a story they they previously binged on from the comfort of their couch. This iteration of “Evil Genius,” like its nonfiction predecessor, would make most sense as streaming fodder, with potential Emmy catnip in Arquette’s offputting but undeniably attention-grabbing characterization. As a gala Toronto premiere, however, the film felt a little small for the room.
	

	The core details of the case are presented much as they were in the doc series and copious headlines before it. On August 28, 2003, middle-aged pizza deliverer Brian Wells (played by actor-filmmaker Tom McCarthy as a hopeless patsy) robbed a branch of PNC Bank outside Erie, Pennsylvania, claiming to be a hostage, with an explosive device collared to his neck that he said would be detonated if his demands were not met. Demanding $250,000 but making off with a four-figure sum, he was apprehended shortly afterwards by police, whereupon the bomb did indeed go off, killing him, and cuing a tortuous, years-long FBI investigation.

	Structurally, at least, this calamity serves as the climax of the frenetically pinballing script by Courtenay Miles (a writer on Netflix’s hit crime drama “Mindhunter”), but it’s also nearly incidental to all the other narrative chaos at play, beginning with an entirely different murder at the outset of proceedings — as Rothstein calls the police to report the dead body of Diehl-Armstrong’s boyfriend in her freezer. Where the series worked backwards from the bomb to uncover the botched grand plan behind it, the film loopily joins the dots from an apparent crime of passion to a far more famous crime of greed. 

	There’s an awful lot of incident here to cram into 97 minutes — the series had more than twice as much time to unfold this saga, and the difference is felt — but Cox’s film distinguishes itself with a greater focus on the toxic, on-off amour fou between Diehl-Armstrong, presented here as an embittered harridan convinced the world owes her a break, and Rothstein, the hapless milquetoast in her thrall. Flashbacks to the characters’ youth (with Arquette’s own daughter Harlow Jane playing her younger self) identify Diehl-Rothstein as an intelligent, ingenuous young woman who just needs a little help to make something of herself. But neither the script nor Arquette’s showy but curdled, stridently one-note performance of terminal misanthropy persuasively draw a line between past and present, and it’s increasingly hard to feel for a character missing this much connective tissue.

	Not that feeling is really the point of “Evil Genius,” which mostly dwells on the shouty, combative dysfunction of the relationship between the two principals, and punches down on their plain incapability as criminals: The title is strictly, snidely ironic, as “Evil Genius” flags and foreshadows their every miscalculation with a knowing, get-a-load-of-this smirk. Their accomplices — played by Garret Dillahunt and Danielle Macdonald, among others — are mostly figures of fun, granted limited personality and motivation, as the film increasingly stages their doomed venture as ragged farce. 
	

	Tonally, it all feels a bit over-egged: The absurdities of the case would, if anything, register even more startlingly in a more humane, character-oriented study of how it played out. But “Evil Genius” insists on casting a pretty ugly story in the ugliest possible light — quite literally so in the case of Eigil Bryld’s intentionally harsh, roughly framed lensing. The film’s pitiless gray images compete with the abrasive sound design (frequently submerging the dialogue in loud, blunt needle drops that run the rock gamut from Blue Oyster Cult to Radiohead) for maximum unloveliness in a story that, yes, offers precious little scope for grace or beauty. But a little empathy wouldn’t go amiss.

schema.headline: ‘Evil Genius’ Review: Courteney Cox Fashions the Pizza Bomber Case Into a Broad, Shrilly Played Farce

title: Rei Ami on Her New Pop Girl Era, and How Feeling Confident Inspired Her New Single ‘2 Loud’: ‘It’s a Clapback’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Rei Ami is loving life, and she’s also learned to love herself. But it wasn’t an easy journey getting to this stage. 

	Before breaking out as one-t
body:
Rei Ami is loving life, and she’s also learned to love herself. But it wasn’t an easy journey getting to this stage. 

	Before breaking out as one-third of Huntr/x in Netflix’s smash “KPop Demon Hunters,” Ami largely released rap songs like “Snow Cone” and “Body Bag,” which she says came from a place of anger and resentment. But following the release of “Hunters,” which won her both an Oscar and a Grammy, the 31-year-old found a new path forward.
	

	“I think the ‘KPop Demon Hunters’ campaign healed something in me,” Ami tells Variety. “It shifted and changed a lot for me.” After the film introduced the singer-songwriter to a new generation of fans and propelled her to another stratosphere of stardom, it also unlocked a new era of confidence and self-acceptance, something reflected in her latest single “2 Loud,” a brassy pop anthem for the dance floor-sounding song releasing this Friday.


	“2 Loud” signals a shift in her music, influenced by Ami’s inner pop girl. Here, Ami speaks with Variety about this new chapter and sound, and what to expect from her in the near future.
	
		This is a new era for you, and there’s so much confidence in this song. You can hear it in the lyrics. Where did that shift happen?	

	We’ve chatted so many times. You saw me and the girls throughout the campaign, and it was crazy. I’ve never been thrust into that level of visibility in my life. I’ve never had people online comment about just me existing. And I had to process so many things all at once. I’ve had to develop new habits, like not reading the comments and putting a pause on the doomscrolling.
	

	At one point, I read a comment about one of our performances, and it said, “She’s doing too much.” I thought, “How am I doing too much?” I am in a position where millions of people are watching me. I have an opportunity of a lifetime. You want me to not do my job, right? What are you even talking about? 

	And it made me think: These people don’t actually know me. Sometimes, you just have to let it be. You don’t have to understand why they would comment such a bizarre thing, but they do, and that’s not my problem. 

	It made me realize that me being “too much” has opened so many opportunities for me. It has given me the ability to change my life and change my parents’ lives. So I channeled this feeling that’s been weighing on my heart for so long into a song, and that became “2 Loud.” 

	I am just so unapologetically me. I love myself, and I accept myself—flaws and all—for what and who I am, because it has brought me this far. I am human. I’m imperfect. But so are you. 
	
		I love how you’re embracing that. “2 Loud” is definitely a statement, but also a different vibe. It’s fully you embracing your pop girl side. Talk about this new sound.	

	I’ve been raised by the pop girls — Rihanna, Britney Spears, you name it. I’ve always been a pop girl to the core.

	When I was releasing “Snow Cone” and “Body Bag,” I was in a very dark place in my life. I was still figuring it out. I was angry, resentful, and bitter about so many things in my career and personal life. I think that’s normal and human, and it’s only natural as an artist that I poured it into my work. 

	With “2 Loud,” I’m no longer angry. I’ve let go of a lot. I want to dance. I want to celebrate life. I want to live life. I want to express myself. That’s what I am prioritizing in my life: happiness, joy, and being able to live this blessing of a life to the fullest, as my most authentic, truest self. 

	And that’s what “2 Loud” is about. That’s what I want to usher into this new era of music — this freedom to be human. I think that’s what everyone wants. They want to feel human, to feel heard and connected. And I think that’s what the world needs right now.
	
		It’s a very fun pop tune. I heard that you were inspired to go into the studio after the 20th anniversary of “Hannah Montana.” Is that true?	

	It’s so funny because we’re actually releasing on the same day as Miley’s album, which is, again, synchronistic. My co-writers, producers, and executive producer were already setting up shop at the studio because that week I was going to start writing camp. But there was something in me that said, “Let’s stop by the studio.” 
	

	So I went there, and they had already started building out “2 Loud.” My co-writer, Maia Kelly, was already writing the verse, and she had tracked it. We were talking about it because, at the time, I really was feeling it. I was like, “Oh my God, am I too much?”

	I’ve been really in my head, asking: “Am I losing myself? Am I becoming something I’m not?” But I also have a new audience now—children — and I have to be considerate. I’m part of something bigger than me. All these thoughts kept me overanalyzing and second-guessing everything. I was losing my mind. Maia and I were talking, and she said, “Too loud, too much — let’s just fucking talk about it.”

	The next day, I wrote the second verse. I went in because I was pissed. I thought, “I’m not safe for your work. My old shit? Definitely not safe for your kids. It’s not even PG-13. It’s rated R for Rei Ami.” So we tracked it, and as I was listening to it, I thought, “This is everything I’ve wanted to say for a minute now.” It’s a clapback. It’s essentially saying, “Y’all don’t actually fucking know me. You don’t know what ‘too loud’ is. You haven’t seen loud.” If this is too loud for you, ooh, I can’t fucking wait for you to see what’s coming next. If you don’t like it, turn it off.



	

	


	
		This is you being your authentic self. How much of a creative explosion has this been for you?	

	This album is my story as an artist. There’s nothing really profound or philosophical about it. It’s very honest and human. It’s every high and low that I’ve experienced, and it’s just me talking about the things that matter to me and have affected me. I think many people are going to relate to that. It’s told through the lens of my life and my human experience, but it’s a very universal album. 
	
	
		How has writing these songs, especially “2 Loud,” healed you?	

	It’s made me more confident and self-assured in who I am and in my gut intuition. When you’re confident and you know what you want, the vision becomes a little clearer. I urge people to find confidence wherever they can because it can heal so many parts of you. A lot of the things we shame ourselves for are the things that could really change our lives and our futures. For me, being loud or extra—I dimmed that part of myself heavily. Growing up in a religious environment, there was a lot of suppression. It was disgusting and evil. But the moment I let her out, people found it charming. And especially in this kind of career, it really helped.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: Rei Ami on Her New Pop Girl Era, and How Feeling Confident Inspired Her New Single ‘2 Loud’: ‘It’s a Clapback’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Star Hudson Williams Sparks TIFF Chaos, Teases Season 2
description:
It’s been a whirlwind year for Hudson Williams.

	Ever since “Heated Rivalry,” Jacob Tierney’s sensuous decade-long romantic saga between closeted h
body:
It’s been a whirlwind year for Hudson Williams.

	Ever since “Heated Rivalry,” Jacob Tierney’s sensuous decade-long romantic saga between closeted hockey stars Shane Hollander (Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie), premiered in November 2025 on Crave and HBO Max, Williams has been thrust into the spotlight. Adapted from Rachel Reid’s “Game Changers” series of novels exploring toxic masculinity, internalized homophobia and the closet, and providing an addictive mélange of yearning and forbidden love, “Heated Rivalry” became a global phenomenon, earning Williams Best Leading Performance in a Drama Series at the 2026 Canadian Screen Awards (the youngest winner ever at 25) for his sensitive portrayal of the autistic Hollander, and vaulting its two magnetic leads to the A-list.
	

	The tabloid scrutiny has also led to some unfortunate episodes, however, like the time Williams was followed to his apartment in Paris by a rabid gang of autograph hounds and the gossip blogs’ fixation on his relationship with his long-term girlfriend Katelyn Larson.


	On Sept. 17, the hometown boy appeared at the Toronto International Film Festival for “Making Waves With … Hudson Williams,” a career-spanning conversation with TIFF’s vice president of public programming, Keith Bennie, at the Royal Alexandra Theatre in downtown Toronto. Williams was on hand to promote his role in “Yaga,” an upcoming horror series from Kat Sandler premiering Oct. 23 on Crave and AMC. And the talk drew far and away the longest lines of the festival, snaking around four city blocks an hour before showtime. The situation didn’t improve upon arrival at the theater, with the ushers’ ticket readers broken and unable to scan people in. The logistical hiccups caused the talk to begin late (a running theme at this year’s fest). Once it did, though, all seemed forgiven, as the actor was showered with more “Woos!” and “We love you’s!” than the rest of the festival’s talks combined.
	

	The talk began with Bennie asking Williams about attending a screening of “Obsession” at TIFF. According to Williams, he’d already seen the film before, but he and star Inde Navarrette share a lawyer, so he went to see it again — and was just as scared this time. And he’s a big horror fan.

	“I love horror. I could be up here for a long time talking about my favorite horror movies, but it’s definitely a genre I want to get into,” he said. “I think I had a high horror threshold when I was a kid, so I was looking for something that could truly rattle me.”

	Williams opened up about his early years going to a performing arts elementary school where the kids performed “dumbed-down Shakespeare” and “poetry recitals,” which laid the foundation for revisiting acting in high school and beyond. He said his biggest inspiration as a young actor was Heath Ledger’s turn as The Joker in “The Dark Knight.” The audience was also treated to Williams’ short films, including “Dogging,” a documentary spoof featuring him in underwear and a dog collar as a man grieving his overbearing mother’s death who’s being rented out by people and treated as a dog.

	“All of us were working jobs. We did not get paid to do anything. But that’s what brought us all together. We wanted to make things that were fun to us and challenged us in different ways, even though they were completely ridiculous,” Williams explained.

	At one point, Williams fielded a question from Tierney about his “least favorite movie,” and confessed that it was David Ayer’s 2016 superhero flick “Suicide Squad.”

	“The first ‘Suicide Squad’ I was excited for … the trailer was so good and I was just disappointed,” he admitted, adding diplomatically, “Everyone who’s in it was good!”

	Eventually, the talk turned to “Heated Rivalry.” Williams said he was “just waiting by a phone for five years with no promise of it going well, but obviously ‘Heated Rivalry’ changed things.” The audience was shown a clip of Hollander coming out to his girlfriend Sophie, played by Sophie Nélisse. Williams was asked by Bennie about playing someone so deep in the closet and delivering such a remarkably restrained performance.

	“Underneath, I think it’s the excruciating pain of knowing exactly who you are and what you like and it reading as wrong up here, and those two things being so out of tune and not being able to go, ‘I know what I am … and that is OK,’” Williams said of Hollander’s internal struggle.
	

	“It was clear to me that Shane has never been vulnerable in front of another person about the biggest thing that looms over him and has followed him for over a decade,” Williams continued, “and Sophie/Rose makes it so easy, but he’s not comfortable feeling that vulnerable, so [I was] just trapping it underneath the surface and making sure you’re feeling all of it.”

	Williams had kind words for “Heated Rivalry’s” feverish fans and how they picked up on exactly what he was trying to accomplish with his depiction of Hollander, particularly the way he grappled with his feelings for Rozanov and his inability to tell him how he truly feels.

	“This guy’s kind of this little loser boy. You’re kind of like, come on, man! Just tell him! Stand up for yourself! Stop giving in! Say what you’re feeling!” joked Williams. “And he doesn’t do it. He’s just too fucking smitten. But they somehow picked up on all the things that I was using to justify why he’s not standing up for himself.”

	He briefly teased Season 2 of “Heated Rivalry,” which is currently filming and expected to hit screens in April 2027, saying it was “surreal” to step into Hollander’s shoes (skates?) once more and emphasizing its difference in tone and approach.

	“It’s a sad book. If Season 1/Book 1 is the yearning season, Book 2 is external adversity and interrelational communication problems that feel very real and human,” offered Williams. “Just to be able to play those as Shane is going to be frustrating and annoying to leave set with things that are left unsaid, but hopefully it will make for good TV.”

schema.headline: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Star Hudson Williams Sparks TIFF Chaos, Teases Season 2

title: Miley Cyrus Describes Last Conversation With Dolly Parton, Prompted by Sending Over Her New Album: ‘Though We Were So Different, That’s What Made Us Perfect for Each Other’
description: Miley Cyrus, now being professionally known as just Miley, spoke about her last conversation with her godmother, Dolly Parton — stemming from Cyrus
body:
Miley Cyrus, now being professionally known as just Miley, spoke about her last conversation with her godmother, Dolly Parton — stemming from Cyrus sending Parton an advance copy of her new album, “Bass Persuades” — in a fresh interview with Zane Lowe.

	“Dolly has been the first person that when I get a vinyl printed,” Parton told the Apple Music podcast host. “That’s the first person I send it to since I’ve been making vinyls, and this time around I was going to send her a vinyl because I always do. I’m just trying to keep myself together, but the time that we talked, which was the last time we would talk, it was actually me telling her about this record because even though we are so different, that’s what made us so perfect for each other, It’s that — and she knew this, and I know this — she is known for the fake, the hair, the makeup, and the show of it. But there’s a part of her that I think is what everyone gravitates towards… how real she is and how authentic she is. 
	

	“And there was a time in my life — we hit on it with Hannah (Montana) — so much of my life was about persona. And I think a way that I could look at that as you can have a persona and still be who you are is because I had Dolly. Sometimes I call what I do drag because the way that I present myself is just someone that is so different from the person that feeds the tortoise every morning. But again, that person’s inside of me. I just kind of have her off. One of the things we talked about was, in my performances, I always cry; I can’t help it. (SInging) ‘End of the World,’ I start crying and she watched me on Letterman and was like, ‘What are you crying about?’ That song’s about the world ending and me never seeing my mom again.”
	

	Lowe suggested that maybe what Parton was trying to tell her was: You need to be more professional.

	“That’s pretty much what she said,” responded Cyrus. “She was like, ‘Music is escapism. Let them cry. You need to get through it.’ And I was like, ‘I know, but this is who I am.’ And she loved me for it,” despite their different takes on how emotional to get in public.Cyrus discussed having a keen sense of how the role models she has had in her life will eventually disappear from it, as Parton has.

	“I cried singing ‘I Will Always Love You’ with her,” she said, “but I think she knew at that time that the reason I was crying is the reason that I cry now, which is because so many of my really stabilizing peers that I have in my life [come from] generations before me. And they’ve laid down, brick by brick, the road that I travel now. And they aren’t always going to be here for me to call them and say, ‘What do I do now?,’ which I always did with Dolly. And she was always right. It’s like how your mom’s like always right, and when you’re a kid, you’re like, what does she know? And then as you get older, you’re like, ‘How? Where did this come from? You’re just a normal person. Why do you know everything?’ Dolly was just always right about stuff.”

	Cyrus’ new album comes out at midnight Thursday night. She described how producer Max Martin convinced her to go for a certain upbeat and propulsive sound on the album, which she resisted, at least for songs that were conceived as ballads.

	Of a track called “Aftermath,” Cyrus said, “A funny story about that song: one of the lyrics actually says ‘the Titan sinks,’ so it was actually about a submarine, and I wrote it as a very sad ballad. I was playing a bunch of the songs that I had written, because I wrote them a little differently this record, and I was playing the record as it was with Max and I said, ‘Is there anything? Like, be brutal, tell me what you don’t like.’ He was like, ‘God, that “Aftermath” song is boring. I’m just going to be honest with you.’ He’s like, ‘So boring.’ So [I say] ‘What would you do with it?’ And then boom, boom, boom, boom and I was like, that is better. I was going for the Thom Yorke-like vibe, but he’s like, ‘No, boring.’ So he made that song so much better.”

	”

schema.headline: Miley Cyrus Describes Last Conversation With Dolly Parton, Prompted by Sending Over Her New Album: ‘Though We Were So Different, That’s What Made Us Perfect for Each Other’

title: Eric Schrier Moves to Production Pact as Disney Shakes Up TV Leadership With Adam Smith Taking Full Oversight of Direct to Consumer
description: More changes are coming to Disney‘s top TV ranks as Eric Schrier moves from his role as head of international originals to a production pact amid th
body:
More changes are coming to Disney‘s top TV ranks as Eric Schrier moves from his role as head of international originals to a production pact amid the larger shakeup of Disney TV leadership.

	Earlier Thursday, Disney confirmed a big change as Adam Smith will take over full oversight of direct to consumer operations after previously sharing leadership as co-president with Joe Earley.



	

					Adam Smith and Joe Earley
									Disney
	



	Smith has been named chairman of direct-to-consumer for Disney Entertainment, while Earley is shifting into the newly created role of president of Disney Entertainment Television franchise and content strategy. Smith will report to Disney president and chief creative officer Dana Walden, who announced the news Thursday. Earley will report to Disney Entertainment Television chairman Debra OConnell. 
	

	In a memo to staffers, OConnell addressed the change for Schrier, who joined Disney TV after 22 years as one of the architects of FX.


	“As Eric and I have been talking about the future, he shared with me his desire to return to his creative roots,” she wrote. “After an extraordinary 26 years at Disney, including as one of the early architects of FX, Eric has decided this is the right moment to pursue that next chapter. I’m so pleased that we’ll continue working together through a new producing partnership with DET. Eric plans to share more about what’s ahead soon, and we’re excited about what we’re going to create together.”

	The shake-up comes at a time when Disney is focused on making Disney+ a main focal point for the company. The goal internally is to a structure that creates a single, dedicated leader for the direct-to-consumer business as it continues to scale.
	

	Additional details about the leadership changes will be announced at a later date.

	As chairman, Smith will be responsible for the company’s global entertainment SVOD business, driving strategy, development and continued innovation across the company’s streaming platforms, proprietary advertising technology, emerging technologies and more, per Disney, In his expanded role, Disney says Smith will oversee Disney+ and Hulu, including product, engineering, advertising technology, programming strategy, viewer experience, partnerships and data & analytics.

	In his new role, Earley will lead the strategic development of Disney Entertainment Television franchises, maximizing their value and creating new opportunities to engage audiences and drive the business forward. Earley will oversee all content and production for international originals, production, labor relations and creative talent development.

	After more than 20 years working at Google and YouTube, Smith joined Disney in 2024 as chief product and technology officer for Disney Entertainment and ESPN. He was promoted to co-president of direct-to-consumer alongside Earley back in March.

	“Over the past two years, Adam has done an exceptional job building a world-class team of product and technology leaders and has significantly enhanced the Disney+ user experience globally,” The Walt Disney Company president and chief creative officer Dana Walden said. “Alan Bergman and I are pleased to recognize the tremendous impact he has had on our direct-to-consumer business since he joined Disney, and we are confident that he is the right leader to meet the critical moment we’re in and take us to the next level.”

	“Disney has the best storytellers and the most passionate fandom in the world, and I couldn’t be prouder of what this team has built together,” Smith said. “We’ve established real momentum, and our vision ahead is clear: make Disney+ the connection point for fans everywhere to engage with the full breadth and depth of the broader Disney ecosystem. I’m grateful for this team, energized by what’s ahead, and excited for our next chapter.”

	Most recently co-president of direct-to-consumer and head of content strategy, Earley joined Disney in 2019 to oversee global Disney+ marketing and operations ahead of its launch. He was then named president of Hulu in 2022 and became the head of Disney’s direct-to-consumer division in April 2023. Previously, Earley worked at Fox.
	

	“Joe has been an exceptional leader for our direct-to-consumer business over the past four years, and I am deeply grateful for his partnership and meaningful contributions,” Walden said. “He is a talented executive with a rare combination of business acumen and creative instincts, and Debra OConnell and I could not be more excited to welcome him to the leadership team at Disney Entertainment Television.”

	(Pictured top: Eric Schrier)

schema.headline: Eric Schrier Moves to Production Pact as Disney Shakes Up TV Leadership With Adam Smith Taking Full Oversight of Direct to Consumer

title: ‘Lizzie Borden’ Cast on Treating the Story as a Comedy, the Joy of Playing a Sadistic Character and Finding Empathy for a Bloody Monster: ‘I Understand This Person’

body:
“Don’t you worry: I look after my axes,” Charlie Hunnam says proudly with an impish grin.

	At the moment, he’s not in character but rather marveling at a hobby he picked up before filming “Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story.” In it, he plays Lizzie’s father, an undertaker who is fine chopping a client’s legs off if they are too tall for the coffin.

	Hunnam himself says that in the months leading up to filming, he’d been noticing felled trees on the side of the road while driving through Los Angeles. He took to chopping them up and throwing them into the back of his pickup truck.
	

	“I ended up with probably about 10 tons of wood and bought some great axes and started becoming quite the axeman,” he says. “I’ve been really, really wanting these beautiful Scandinavian axes. When I got this, because Andrew Borden’s an ax collector, I said, ‘Well, it’s for the work. I’ve got to have these axes.’”




	

					Charlie Hunnam as Andrew Borden in “Monster”
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	The conversation mirrors the surprising, irreverent tone of this season of “Monster.” A complete turn from the darkness of “The Ed Gein Story,” in which Hunnam starred as the titular killer, there is a lightness, beauty and levity to Lizzie’s story — even when she grabs an ax and takes some whacks.

	This fourth season stars Ella Beatty as the naive, curious title character, whose world brightens when a new housemaid, Bridget Sullivan (Vicky Krieps), arrives and introduces Lizzie to daring literature and kinky sex. Yet her awakening is dampened by her depressed father and cruel stepmother Abby (Rebecca Hall).
	

	Despite Lizzie committing such a legendary crime, Beatty was able to find a kindred spirit in the character, a very complicated young woman.

	“I felt very connected to the character immediately,” she says. “I remember making the audition tape and thinking, ‘I understand this person.’ When I found out that I had gotten the part, I was over the moon and also really scared. I felt a huge responsibility to the part, to the anthology, to the real person. I think immediately I just wanted to start working on it. How does she move? How does she dream? How does she think? How does she speak? How does she blink?”



	

					Rebecca Hall as Abby Borden and Ella Beatty as Lizzie Borden
									Courtesy of Netflix
	



	Hall, whose character says some jaw-droppingly mean things to her stepdaughter, was thrilled to unwrap a deliciously cruel antagonist.

	“I’ve never played a true out-and-out villain,” she says. “I just loved on the page how funny she was. It just felt like such an opportunity to be both funny and scary at the same time, which is an interesting tonal challenge. I loved [writer] Ian Brennan’s take on this character, which felt like it was a creation of Ian Brennan and [executive producer] Ryan Murphy and had nothing to do with history really, as much as it gave me license to create this unique character.”

	Despite Abby’s savagery, Hall saw a unique reflection of the character and the title killers in the series. 

	“Nothing in this ‘Monster’ world is straightforward,” she says. “The exercise of the show is really about how monsters aren’t born, they’re created. So even Abby Borden has that as well. There’s reason behind it. She’s also in a pressure cooker, and she’s become an alcoholic over time. I sort of loved the character. There’s a lot of fun to be had, and there’s something very interesting about playing someone who’s keeping up appearances, who wants to appear posh and together and is just a complete and utter mess — and a sadistic one to boot.”

	This season is a star-making moment for Beatty, whose parents, Annette Bening and Warren Beatty, are legends in their own right. Yet she’s found her way to “Monster” through plenty of time on stage as well as smaller parts in movies such as “If I Had Legs I’d Kick You” and the 2024 Murphy-verse series “Feud: Capote vs. the Swans.”
	

	As the central figure on the show, Beatty says she definitely had nerves but was fascinated to get on the series’ unique wavelength.

	“I knew that they were interested in exploring an almost farcical tone,” she says. “We all just continued to discover it together. It felt a lot more available on set than you might initially think. I was constantly surprised by the ability of comedy and really intense sadness or drama to be in the show. I felt like we discovered it together the whole time.”

	Despite its 19th-century trappings, there is a universality to the story and its outrageousness that Hunnam is excited for audiences to engage with.

	“It felt like there was much more license for a bonkers absurdity that felt like it was on the page and that I was surprised by and really excited about,” he says. “I thought there was a complexity and a tragedy and a nastiness and a vulnerability and all of the things that you look for that are true of all of us.”

	Watch a trailer for “Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story” below.

schema.headline: ‘Lizzie Borden’ Cast on Treating the Story as a Comedy, the Joy of Playing a Sadistic Character and Finding Empathy for a Bloody Monster: ‘I Understand This Person’

title: Spotify Launches Fresh Finds Forward Program to Support Emerging Independent Musicians
description: Spotify is looking to support emerging artists with the launch of Fresh Finds Forward, a program intended to give roughly 10,000 independent artists
body:
Spotify is looking to support emerging artists with the launch of Fresh Finds Forward, a program intended to give roughly 10,000 independent artists support and resources each year.

	The streaming service shared details of the program, allowing any artist added to Fresh Finds playlists from January 1, 2026 to join Fresh Finds Forward via Spotify for Artists. Once onboarded into the program, musicians will have access to resources for 12 months, including free studio time for U.S.-based artists at locations like New York City’s Electric Lady Studios; early utilization of some Spotify tools and features; and mental health resources and free therapy for six months via BetterHelp.
	

	Fresh Finds playlists have been active on Spotify for more than a decade, providing a platform for over 80,000 artists across 127 countries. Early placements have ranged from Laufey and Clairo to Ethel Cain and Omar Apollo. Since 2024, these playlists have driven over 128 million new artist discoveries, and more than half of the artists end up being programmed on other editorial playlists.


	“Fresh Finds has always been about finding artists at a pivotal moment and helping them reach new audiences at the right time,” said Joe Hadley, Spotify’s global head of music content and partnerships. “We spent years listening to what independent artists actually need, and those conversations shaped what this program would become. Fresh Finds Forward takes everything we’ve learned from a decade of discovery and builds a support system around it, so participating artists aren’t just getting a playlist placement, they’re getting the benefits, resources, and the community to make the most of that moment.”

schema.headline: Spotify Launches Fresh Finds Forward Program to Support Emerging Independent Musicians

            Samuel Monroe Jr. -- famous for his work in "Menace II Society" -- died of respiratory failure and meningitis ... with pneumonia also playing a role.
      
    
            TMZ obtained the actor's death certificate ... and it states Samuel's cause of death was respiratory failure and a coccidioidal meningitis infection.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sepsis pneumonia is listed as a contributing factor ... and the doc states he's been buried at a Los Angeles cemetery.
      

            As we reported ... Joyce Patton -- Samuel's mom -- told us he died last month. Sam was hospitalized with a severe case of meningitis and MRSA pneumonia in April. On Facebook, she asked fans to pray for his family, especially his 3 kids.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            In addition to 'M2S,' Samuel Monroe Jr. also appeared in "Tales From The Hood," "Set It Off," "Don't Be a Menace to South Central While Drinking Your Juice in the Hood" and "The Player's Club."
      
    
            Shawna Stewart -- who told us she was Samuel's wife -- had his power of attorney and was in charge of his finances at the time of his death. She's listed on the death certificate as well.
      
    
            He was 52.

body:
'That's So Raven' Star
                          Bobb'e J. Thompson Gets 30 Months In Federal Prison
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 17, 2026
                            2:50 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Bobb'e J. Thompson -- a former child star known for playing Stanley on "That's So Raven" -- has been sentenced to 30 months in prison after pleading guilty to a gun charge.
      
    
            A judge in Iowa handed down the sentence on Thursday ... almost one year after cops say they pulled him over going 104 MPH in a 70 MPH zone.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Cops say they searched Thompson's bag during the stop and found packages of marijuana purchased at a dispensary and a loaded .40-caliber handgun ... which was allegedly stolen from a car in Kansas City, MO.
      
    
            Thompson pled guilty to the charge back in April. He has been ordered to serve 30 months in federal prison ... and will be on 3 years of supervised release once he gets out.
      
    
            He's currently in the custody of U.S. Marshals ... until he's transferred to a federal prison.
      
    
            In addition to "That's So Raven," Bobb'e also appeared in a bunch of movies ... including "Role Models," "Me and Earl and the Dying Girl" and "Shark Tale" ... plus TV shows like "The Tracy Morgan Show," "30 Rock" and "Wild 'n Out."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Thompson's dealt with numerous legal issues since he stopped acting years ago.
      
    
            Prosecutors say in 2022 he was convicted of battery causing serious bodily injury, assault, and prohibited firearm possession.

title: Haley Kalil Ex-Husband Matt's Penis Size Lawsuit Dismissed
description:
Haley Kalil
                          Court Dismisses Ex-Husband's Penis Size Lawsuit
body:
Haley Kalil
                          Court Dismisses Ex-Husband's Penis Size Lawsuit
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 17, 2026
                            12:17 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 17, 2026
                                1:21 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A judge has granted Haley Kalil's request to throw out her ex-husband Matt Kalil's lawsuit ... after she claimed his huge penis ended their marriage.
      
    
            Haley tells TMZ ... "I am so relieved this is over. I never wanted to be in a courtroom discussing matters of my own life. I think this ruling is important and I hope it encourages women everywhere to speak openly about what they've been through. Your story belongs to you and you shouldn’t fear sharing it."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Haley's attorney, Matthew Bialick, tells TMZ ... "We are very pleased that the Court dismissed every count against Haley."
      

            We previously reported ... Haley claimed in July that she never mentioned her former husband by name when she went on a live stream and described her ex's penis as two stacked Coca-Cola cans.
      
    
            In his initial filing, Matt claimed Haley's "invasive commentary" ruined his attempt at staying out of the public eye following his retirement -- in response, Haley said he was only identifiable from her remarks because she and Matt are both public figures.
      
    
            And Haley's legal team had argued that because they were public figures, the reasons behind her divorce were matters of public interest.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Speaking out about the ruling, Matthew wrote ... "The Court found that Haley was speaking about her body, her life, and her marriage. She was talking about the trauma she went through and what led to her divorce. Those experiences are hers, and she has every right to talk about them."
      
    
            He added ... "No woman should need her ex-husband's permission to tell the story of her own marriage. No woman should be sued for talking about her own body. We hope this ruling gives women everywhere the confidence to share their own stories."
